cards.front: A protein that converts a stimulus into an electrical signal is a {{c1::transducer}}.
cards.back: Temperature-gated ion channels serve this role in thermosensation.
cards.quote: A transducer is the protein that turns a stimulus into an electrical signal;

cards.front: What distinguishes innocuous from noxious temperatures?
cards.back: Innocuous temperatures do not threaten tissue; noxious temperatures damage or threaten to damage it and usually hurt.
cards.quote: Innocuous temperatures, warm or cool, do not threaten the tissue; noxious ones damage or threaten to damage it, and usually hurt.

cards.front: How do C and Aδ sensory fibres differ in myelination and conduction speed?
cards.back: C fibres are unmyelinated and slowly conducting; Aδ fibres are thinly myelinated and conduct faster.
cards.quote: C fibres are thin, unmyelinated and slowly conducting. Aδ fibres ("A-delta") are thinly myelinated and conduct faster.
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: The channel activated by noxious heat and capsaicin is {{c1::TRPV1}}.
cards.back: Capsaicin is the hot molecule in chilli.
cards.quote: TRPV1 opens with noxious heat and with capsaicin, the hot molecule in chilli;
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: Cooling and menthol activate {{c1::TRPM8}}.
cards.back: It is the main established transducer of innocuous cooling, not of all cold.
cards.quote: TRPM8 opens with cooling and with menthol;
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: A gene makes a previously unresponsive foreign cell respond to a stimulus. What does this establish about the encoded protein?
cards.back: Molecular sufficiency in that cell. It does not establish necessity in an intact animal or locate the stimulus sensor within the protein.
cards.quote: It tests molecular sufficiency: this protein, in this foreign cell, responds to this stimulus.
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: Which readout selected a candidate TRPV1 clone from sensory-neuron cDNA pools expressed in foreign cells?
cards.back: Capsaicin-evoked calcium influx.
cards.quote: expressed pools of sensory-neuron cDNA in cells that do not normally respond to capsaicin and screened for capsaicin-evoked calcium influx
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: Why does loss of TRPM8 not establish that all cold sensing requires TRPM8?
cards.back: TRPM8-null mice have greatly reduced cold responses but still avoid surfaces below 10 °C; other routes must support that avoidance.
cards.quote: Mice lacking TRPM8 have profoundly reduced cold responses in neurons and fibres, yet they still avoid surfaces below 10 °C
cards.section: The map: ranges, fibres and channels

cards.front: With the stimulated skin patch held at 32 °C, what activity did a 27 °C bath reveal in isolated mouse forepaw skin that a 32 °C bath had not?
cards.back: The cooler bath exposed cool-sensitive C fibres firing at rest, allowing warming-induced suppression to be seen; awake forepaw skin measured 26 to 28 °C.
cards.quote: At the usual 32 °C bath, no such fibres had been seen.
cards.section: Lines that fire at rest

cards.front: Two sensory fibres respond to cooling by increasing firing. One is silent at rest; the other fires steadily. If warming is encoded by a rate decrease, which can signal it and why?
cards.back: Only the steadily firing fibre can signal warming by slowing down. The silent fibre has no baseline spikes to lose.
cards.quote: A fibre that is silent at rest can report a change only by starting to fire.
cards.section: Lines that fire at rest

cards.front: How do the two warmth-responsive C-fibre populations in mouse forepaw skin change firing during warming?
cards.back: Warm-excited polymodal C fibres increase firing, while cool-sensitive C fibres reduce ongoing firing. Warmth therefore involves changes in more than one afferent line.
cards.quote: Two kinds of C fibre answered warming, in opposite directions.
cards.section: The signature response

cards.front: A sensory fibre responsive to multiple kinds of stimulus is called {{c1::polymodal}}.
cards.back: For example, a temperature-responsive fibre may also respond to pressure.
cards.quote: Polymodal means the fibre also responds to other kinds of stimulus, such as pressure.
cards.section: The signature response

cards.front: In a lick-report detection task, licking on a no-stimulus catch trial is a {{c1::false alarm}}.
cards.back: Catch trials measure reports made without the stimulus.
cards.quote: a lick on a catch trial is a false alarm.
cards.section: Measuring detection: hits, false alarms and d′

cards.front: The signal-detection sensitivity index is d′ = z(hit rate) − {{c1::z(false-alarm rate)}}.
cards.back: z converts a probability to a standard-normal z score; d′ is dimensionless.
cards.quote: d′ = z(hit rate) − z(false-alarm rate)
cards.section: Measuring detection: hits, false alarms and d′

cards.front: In a constructed warming-detection session, a mouse licks on 80 of 100 warming trials and 10 of 100 catch trials. Given z(0.80) = 0.8416 and z(0.10) = −1.282, calculate d′.
cards.quote: It is a sensitivity index, not a temperature:
cards.section: Measuring detection: hits, false alarms and d′

cards.front: Why can hit rate alone overstate sensitivity in a detection task?
cards.back: A subject can score many hits by reporting on nearly every trial. False alarms reveal this readiness to report, allowing sensitivity to be distinguished from criterion.
cards.quote: A mouse that licked on every trial would score hits without detecting anything,
cards.section: Measuring detection: hits, false alarms and d′

cards.front: In an equal-variance signal-detection model with a stable criterion within each session, a criterion shift raises z(hit rate) and z(false-alarm rate) equally. What happens to d′ and why?
cards.back: d′ stays unchanged because it is the difference of the two z scores; equal shifts cancel.
cards.quote: a change in readiness to lick shifts both z scores equally, so their difference measures sensitivity apart from that readiness.
cards.section: Measuring detection: hits, false alarms and d′

cards.front: Why can deleting the cool-activated channel TRPM8 abolish warming reports in the mouse forepaw task?
cards.back: Deleting TRPM8 removes ongoing cool-afferent firing, leaving warming no cool input to reduce. Retained warm-excited fibres were insufficient for reporting in this task.
cards.quote: Without TRPM8 the cool fibres lose their ongoing firing, so warming has nothing left to reduce.
cards.section: Take away the cool line

cards.front: An animal lacking a sensory protein fails a temperature-report task but learns a touch-report task. Local, reversible blockade of that protein in controls also impairs temperature reports. What explanation is strengthened?
cards.back: A sensory contribution is strengthened: successful touch learning argues against a general learning failure, and reversible local blockade supports a role in the sensory response.
cards.quote: Two observations support a sensory explanation: the same mutants readily learned to report mechanical stimuli to the forepaw,
cards.section: Take away the cool line

cards.front: An independent-cue model predicts that retained warm-excited input alone should permit mouse forepaw warming detection after TRPM8 loss. Reports instead fail despite retained warm-excited fibres. Which claim fails, and what remains open?
cards.back: The model’s assumptions fail: an independent, sufficient retained cue should preserve some sensitivity. The data do not identify a unique alternative readout or a central sign-inverting circuit.
cards.quote: On the simplest picture, each line an independent alarm sufficient to drive a report,
cards.section: Take away the cool line

cards.front: Isolated mouse forepaw skin shows warming-induced cool-fibre suppression, and a separate behavioral task requires TRPM8. What additional recording would strengthen the link without identifying a central circuit?
cards.back: Record the cool afferents during warming reports in behaving mice. The rule is that joining separate preparations is an inference; measuring suppression during the task would strengthen that link.
cards.quote: an inference that joins two preparations, not a recording made during the task.
cards.section: Take away the cool line

cards.front: Acute TRPV1 blockade eliminates imaged oral warmth responses in anaesthetized mice, but TRPV1-null mice still report forepaw warming. Do these results isolate body site as the cause of the difference?
cards.back: No. Body site, anaesthesia, measurement and acute blockade versus germline deletion differ. Developmental compensation is possible; these preparations do not isolate a body-site effect.
cards.quote: one blocked TRPV1 acutely with a drug in an anaesthetized animal, the other removed the gene from the start,
cards.section: Take away the cool line

cards.front: Three hypothetical sensors could form an obligatory series chain or provide redundant parallel routes for a reflex. If deleting any one preserves the reflex, but deleting all abolishes it, which arrangement fits and why?
cards.back: Redundant parallel routes fit. An obligatory series chain predicts failure after any single deletion; alternative parallel routes can sustain the reflex when one sensor is lost.
cards.quote: In series, each single knockout would abolish withdrawal, and single knockouts do not.
cards.section: Three channels for one burn: redundancy, not a chain

cards.front: What does combined deletion of TRPV1, TRPM3 and TRPA1 establish about acute noxious-heat withdrawal in the tested mouse assays?
cards.back: These channels are functionally redundant for acute withdrawal: single losses leave responses, whereas combined loss of all three abolishes the tested reflex.
cards.quote: The channels are functionally redundant for this assay: remove one and the others carry the signal,
cards.section: Three channels for one burn: redundancy, not a chain

cards.front: A mouse lacking TRPV1, TRPM3 and TRPA1 retains moderate-temperature preference. Would that predict intact acute noxious-heat withdrawal? Explain.
cards.back: No. Preference and acute withdrawal have different requirements; preference can survive even when the tested heat-withdrawal reflex is lost.
cards.quote: Acute nociceptive withdrawal and graded thermal preference are different behaviours with different requirements,
cards.section: Three channels for one burn: redundancy, not a chain

cards.front: How do mouse spinal heat-responding and cold-responding populations differ in temporal coding?
cards.back: Heat-responding neurons encode absolute skin temperature without adapting; cold-responding neurons adapt quickly and encode temperature change.
cards.quote: heat-responding neurons encode absolute skin temperature without adapting and receive TRPV1-positive input, while cold-responding neurons adapt quickly and encode temperature change
cards.section: Reading the lines: spinal cord, ganglia and insular cortex

cards.front: During hindpaw stimulation in anaesthetized mice, rising temperature recruits additional DRG heat-responsive neurons, while cooling responses are largely ungraded. What coding interpretation fits?
cards.back: Heat has a graded population signal through recruitment. Cooling may use combinatorial coding: which cells respond, rather than how strongly each responds. The cooling interpretation remains suggestive.
cards.quote: Cooling responses were largely ungraded, which the authors read as suggesting combinatorial cold coding:
cards.section: Reading the lines: spinal cord, ganglia and insular cortex

cards.front: A neural map in which neighbouring body parts map to neighbouring neural locations is {{c1::somatotopic}}.
cards.back: This describes the spatial arrangement of a body map.
cards.quote: neighbouring parts of the body mapped to neighbouring cortex
cards.section: Reading the lines: spinal cord, ganglia and insular cortex

cards.front: Why does a cooling-only widefield response in mouse S1 not establish that S1 has no warmth-responsive neurons?
cards.back: Two-photon imaging revealed sparse warmth-responsive neurons in S1. A population-level widefield result need not capture a sparse responding subset.
cards.quote: with only sparse warm-responding neurons under two-photon imaging.
cards.section: Reading the lines: spinal cord, ganglia and insular cortex

cards.front: During awake mouse forepaw reporting, posterior-insula inhibition lowers warming hit rates at every tested amplitude and cooling hit rates only for small tested steps. What causal conclusion fits?
cards.back: Posterior insula contributes to the tested reports, with amplitude-dependent effects. Acute, incomplete inhibition does not prove strict necessity, exclusivity or absence of contribution at the spared large cooling step.
cards.quote: It establishes a causal contribution to the behaviour tested, in this preparation, at those amplitudes;
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the awake mouse forepaw task, posterior-insula inhibition spares detection of a 10 °C cooling step. How could a follow-up distinguish a sufficient parallel route from a ceiling hiding a deficit?
cards.back: Test nearby amplitudes and discrimination between large steps to push performance away from ceiling. The rule is that spared detection fits either parallel sufficiency or enough residual signal to cross threshold.
cards.quote: add a second task where the mouse must tell two large steps apart rather than simply detect one, so the ceiling is pushed away.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Silencing a brain region reduces licking to temperature stimuli. What control would help distinguish impaired sensory reporting from impaired licking?
cards.back: Test an equally demanding nonthermal detection task under the same silencing, with lick measurements. Preserved performance argues against a general motor explanation for fewer temperature reports.
cards.quote: the same light leaves an equally demanding non-thermal detection task intact.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why is apparent Q10 not a fixed temperature-sensing constant of TRPV1?
cards.back: Q10 compares rates 10 °C apart and varies with temperature interval and activation state. Agonist-induced saturation can lower it without changing thermal gating.
cards.quote: The same protein gives different numbers depending on how much agonist has already opened it, so Q10 characterises a state and an interval.
cards.section: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?

cards.front: In an illustrative two-state channel model, an agonist increases opening while thermal gating is held fixed. What happens to the Q10 of open probability as opening approaches saturation, and why?
cards.back: It falls: a channel already mostly open has little room for further opening. The Q10 of the opening equilibrium can remain unchanged, so this does not locate or alter a sensor.
cards.quote: One possible reason is simple: a channel that is already mostly open cannot open much more.
cards.section: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?

cards.front: Why do heat-associated, agonist-bound TRPV1 cryo-EM structures not by themselves locate a temperature sensor?
cards.back: They show conformations under chosen agonist, construct and lipid conditions. Some classes may be off-pathway; structural changes alone do not isolate temperature sensing.
cards.quote: multiple cryo-EM classes may include off-pathway states rather than only sequential intermediates.
cards.section: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?

cards.front: In an illustrative Poisson spike-count model, complete silencing gives D = √(2rT) for resting rate r > 0. For r = 2 Hz and T = 1 s, calculate D. Is this behavioral d′?
cards.back: D = √(2 × 2 × 1) = √4 = 2.00, dimensionless. It separates model spike counts, not hit and false-alarm rates; complete silencing is an assumption, not a measured response to every warming step.
cards.quote: It is computed like d′, but not from hits and false alarms,
cards.section: How much can a fall in firing say?

cards.front: In the illustrative Poisson count model, does a higher resting rate always make a warming-induced decrease easier to distinguish? Compare equal fractional suppression with equal absolute rate drops.
cards.back: No. Equal fractional suppression increases separation with resting rate; equal absolute drops can become less distinct as count variance rises. The rule is that Poisson count variance equals its mean.
cards.quote: If warming removes the same fraction f of spikes, D = f√(rT) / √(1 − f/2);
cards.section: How much can a fall in firing say?

cards.front: Why might different culture durations produce apparent disagreement about the prevalence of warmth-sensitive DRG neurons?
cards.back: Mouse DRG cultures had about 26 ± 9% warmth-sensitive neurons overnight versus about 6 ± 3% after three days. Preparation can change the sampled phenotype.
cards.quote: That roughly fourfold difference between culture protocols, measured in different groups of animals,
cards.section: A culture comparison

cards.front: If opening changes a channel’s heat capacity, must steep temperature sensitivity reside in one compact sensor domain? Explain using the equilibrium model.
cards.back: No. A heat-capacity change makes opening enthalpy vary with temperature, curving ln K against inverse temperature. That thermodynamic rule allows sensitivity distributed across the protein; it does not identify a domain.
cards.quote: A heat-capacity change makes the heat absorbed on opening itself change with temperature, so the line curves.
cards.section: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?

cards.front: A TRPV1 mutation shifts the activation threshold. What paired measurements would help determine whether it changes temperature sensing rather than coupling or general gating?
cards.back: Use the same construct, lipid and fixed voltage across agonist occupancies for structures and Q10, then test sensing, coupling and general gating separately. The rule is that a threshold shift alone cannot distinguish these effects.
cards.quote: A mutation that shifts an activation threshold does not identify a sensor until those three are told apart.
cards.section: What would settle it
